newsitem.title: UK: Physical Lead - A modest pick-up in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Physical Lead - A modest pick-up in Europe.

text.p: Physical lead business has picked up slightly in Europe after the seasonal summer slowdown but the industry is uncertain whether battery demand will surge towards year-end as much as had been expected.
"I think the supply and demand equations are still very much in balance in Europe," an industry source said.

Producer premiums for 99.99 percent purity lead in southern Europe popped up about $10/$15 a several weeks ago when a strike shut Namibia's Tsumeb smelter and Metaleurop had start-up problems at its Nordenham smelter, one trader said.
Metaleurop chairman Helmut Stokieck said on Tuesday that Nordenham would only produce 55 percent of its 90,000 tonnes annual capacity during its first full year of operations.
But premiums have now edged back to an $80 premium over London Metal Exchange cash lead and have remained steady at the same level in northern Europe, the trader added.
Traders said that although seasonal demand had picked up a touch, offtake was softer than expected.
"The market doesn't look too good, I think it's going to remain under pressure," said one, adding that material was being seen from Trepca, the Yugoslav metals giant.
The Belgrade daily Borba reported on Wednesday that Trepca -- which includes 14 lead and zinc mines plus metallurgical plants -- signed a $135 million export deal with a Greek firm.
"I was very, very bullish in the past and I was wrong. To be honest, I don't have a very clear view at the moment," another trader said.
Industry sources said, however, that demand appeared steady, although one acknowledged that he did not have a solid idea of the spot market since all his material was sold on contract.
"My customers are taking all the quantities they contracted for so there must be good demand," said one.
Another industry source said offtake had been good in the first quarter but had been sluggish until now.
"What we are seeing in September is absolutely fine so far. I couldn't say it was exceptional but we're looking for a strong September, October and November," he said.
"A lot of people destocked in the second quarter due to high prices but I think they'll need to stock up now," he added.
The severity of the winter is always key for battery demand, but it was too early to forecast at the moment, sources said.
Traders said metal from Russia and from Kazakhstan dominated stocks at the LME Helsinborg warehouse, which holds the bulk of inventories -- 80,425 tonnes of a total 117,550 tonnes.
Stocks were seen continuing to edge higher, traders said.
Warrant premiums for metal in Rotterdam were said to be $5/$10 over LME cash.
More and more eastern European metal would be consumed within Russia, reducing the impact on the western European market, an industry source said.
"I have heard that the lead premium is higher in Russia than in western Europe so more of the material will be going there," he added.
Two uncertain elements were output of secondary smelters and Chinese production and exports.
"We know more or less the production of the primary lead. Now the question is how is it going to develop with the secondary smelters," a trader said.
An increase in Chinese exports was worrying, MacQuarie Equities said in a commentary this week.
"There are reports of increasing quantities of Chinese lead being offered to Japanese consumers as well as U.S. merchants at very competitive premiums," it said.
Net Chinese exports of refined lead during the first seven months of the year were 130,500 tonnes, nearly double the amount during the same period of 1995, it added.
--Eric Onstad, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8065
